subtitle: Where the algorithms go to work, and what we owe the people affected.

es.body:
Before neural networks took over the headlines, there was a different dream: bottle up what a specialist knows. Imagine a doctor who has seen ten thousand cases, now sitting inside a program. That is an expert system: a specialist’s knowledge captured as if–then rules, plus an inference engine that applies them.

The engine can reason in two directions. Forward chaining starts from the facts and derives conclusions, like a detective collecting clues until a name falls out. Backward chaining starts from a goal (“is it measles?”) and goes looking for the facts that would support it. Add a user interface and an explanation facility that answers “why?”, and you have the full architecture. Classic examples: MYCIN (medical diagnosis) and XCON (configuring computers).

Watch it run. Rules: R1 fever∧rash → measles-suspect; R2 measles-suspect∧contact → measles. Facts: fever, rash, contact. Forward chaining fires R1 first, adding measles-suspect, and that new fact lets R2 fire and add measles. The engine matches rules against facts until nothing new follows. Notice how every step is readable: that is the great strength of rules.
keynotes: An expert system captures a specialist’s knowledge as if–then rules plus an inference engine, a user interface and an explanation facility.
Forward chaining starts from facts and derives conclusions; backward chaining starts from a goal and looks for supporting facts.
Classic examples are MYCIN (medical diagnosis) and XCON (configuring computers).

nlp.body:
“I saw the man with the telescope.” Who has the telescope: you, or the man? Even you can’t tell without more context, and that tiny sentence is the whole difficulty of language in a nutshell.

NLP works through levels, like peeling an onion: phonetic (sounds), morphological (word forms), lexical (words), syntactic (structure, as in parse trees), semantic (meaning) and pragmatic (context and intent). At every level, trouble waits: ambiguity, idiom (“it’s raining cats and dogs”), and context that no sentence carries by itself.

Modern methods take a bold shortcut: pre-train large neural language models on huge amounts of text, then adapt them to translation, summarisation, question answering and dialogue. The model has never been taught grammar; it absorbed it.
keynotes: NLP works through levels: phonetic, morphological, lexical, syntactic (parse trees), semantic and pragmatic.
Challenges include ambiguity (“I saw the man with the telescope”), idiom and context.
Modern methods pre-train large neural language models on huge text and adapt them to translation, summarisation, question answering and dialogue.

vis.body:
How does a robot know there is a pedestrian ahead? Not in one leap. It works through a pipeline, and let’s walk along it once. First acquire an image. Then pre-process it (denoise, normalise). Then extract features: edges, corners, or learned features. Then detect or classify objects, and finally interpret the scene.

A robot adds more around that. It senses with cameras, lidar and encoders; it plans with search and A*, the same ideas from earlier in this course; it controls with feedback loops; and it acts through actuators. Self-driving cars combine every one of those at once.

Spot the pattern in the figure: perceive, plan, act. It’s the agent loop again, the very first picture of this course, now wearing wheels.
keynotes: A vision pipeline acquires an image, pre-processes it, extracts features, detects or classifies objects and interprets the scene.
A robot adds sensing (cameras, lidar, encoders), planning (search, A*), control (feedback loops) and actuators.
Self-driving cars combine all of them in the perceive, plan, act loop.

emerging.body:
Here are three ideas shaping where the field goes next, and each begins with a worry. How do you translate a sentence when the output has a different length from the input? Sequence-to-sequence models turn one sequence into another with an encoder and a decoder, now built with attention.

How do you train a model on people’s phones without ever collecting their private data? Federated learning trains a shared model across many devices: each device computes an update locally, and only the updates are averaged centrally. The raw data never leaves the devices, as the figure shows.

And how do you get an answer without waiting on a network at all? Edge AI runs models on the device itself (phone, camera) for low latency and privacy, using compression such as quantisation and pruning to make the model fit.
keynotes: Sequence-to-sequence models turn one sequence into another with an encoder and decoder, now built with attention.
Federated learning trains a shared model across devices: each computes an update locally and only the updates are averaged centrally, which protects privacy.
Edge AI runs models on the device for low latency and privacy, using compression (quantisation, pruning) to fit.

ethics.body:
A model that is 95% accurate sounds wonderful. Now ask: 95% accurate for whom? Models inherit bias from the data they learn from, and when they are used to make decisions about people, that bias gets a very real cost. Think of unfair decisions in hiring or lending, invasive surveillance, opaque reasoning nobody can challenge, misinformation, and even the energy bill.

So the field has settled on principles: fairness, transparency and explainability, accountability, privacy, safety and robustness, and human oversight. But principles on a poster change nothing; practice does. Audit data and outcomes across groups, document your models, test them adversarially, and keep a human in the loop wherever the stakes are high.

This is why a high overall accuracy can still hide unfairness: the average can look fine while one group is quietly being failed. Always ask who is inside the average.
keynotes: Models inherit bias from data and can harm people: unfair hiring or lending decisions, surveillance, opaque reasoning, misinformation and energy cost.
Principles: fairness, transparency and explainability, accountability, privacy, safety and robustness, human oversight.
Practice: audit data and outcomes across groups, document models, test adversarially and keep a human in high-stakes loops.

sust.body:
Every clever model has a power bill. Training large models consumes large amounts of energy, and “the cloud” is a physical place with real chimneys at the end of the supply chain.

Do the sum once, so it sticks. A training run uses 1000 MWh at 0.4 kg CO₂ per kWh. Convert: 1000 MWh is 10⁶ kWh, so emissions = 10⁶ kWh × 0.4 kg = 4×10⁵ kg, which is 400 tonnes. That is one training run.

What can we do? Use smaller models, apply distillation (a small model learns to mimic a big one), use sparse computation, reuse work through transfer learning, choose efficient hardware, and run in regions with clean energy. Sustainable AI asks one honest question about every project: is the benefit worth the cost?
keynotes: Training large models consumes large amounts of energy.
A run of 1000 MWh at 0.4 kg CO₂ per kWh emits 4×10⁵ kg, which is 400 tonnes.
Efficiency measures: smaller models, distillation, sparse computation, transfer learning, efficient hardware and clean-energy regions.
